name: The Bohr Effect
statement: Acid and carbon dioxide make hemoglobin release oxygen, unloading it where tissues need it most.
meaning: The Bohr effect is the phenomenon by which hemoglobin's oxygen-binding affinity falls as acidity, that is hydrogen-ion concentration, rises and as carbon dioxide rises. An increase in carbon dioxide or a decrease in pH causes hemoglobin to release oxygen more readily, shifting the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. The relationship is reciprocal: just as acid and carbon dioxide promote oxygen release, oxygenation of hemoglobin promotes the release of acid and carbon dioxide. It is an elegant, self-regulating system for delivering oxygen where it is most needed.
mechanism: The effect is allosteric. Hemoglobin exists in a low-affinity tense state and a high-affinity relaxed state. Hydrogen ions protonate specific residues, classically a histidine on the beta chain, letting them form salt bridges that stabilise the tense state and lower oxygen affinity. Carbon dioxide binds directly to the terminal amino groups of the globin chains to form carbamino compounds, which also favour the tense state, and it further lowers pH indirectly through carbonic anhydrase. Because the effect depends on cooperativity between subunits, monomeric myoglobin shows no Bohr effect, confirming its allosteric basis.

examples.text: In active tissue, carbon dioxide and lactic acid accumulate and pH falls, shifting the curve right so hemoglobin unloads more oxygen exactly where demand is greatest, while in the lungs the reverse favours loading.

As carbon dioxide passes from fetal to maternal blood, the fetal side turns relatively alkaline and the maternal side acidic, both shifts favouring the transfer of oxygen from mother to fetus, the double Bohr effect.
The Bohr effect raises P50, the oxygen pressure at which hemoglobin is half saturated, the quantitative signature of a rightward shift and decreased affinity.

variants.name: The reciprocal Haldane effect
variants.text: The counterpart concerning carbon dioxide carriage, in which oxygenation of hemoglobin promotes the release of carbon dioxide; the two are faces of the same allosteric coupling and work together.

variants.name: The double Bohr effect
variants.text: The placental case in which the carbon dioxide shift acidifies maternal and alkalinises fetal blood at once, both changes driving oxygen from mother to fetus.

whyItMatters: It is central to oxygen delivery, exercise physiology, and respiratory physiology, ensuring that oxygen supply is matched to demand: tissues that are working hard, and so producing acid and carbon dioxide, automatically receive more oxygen. It underlies fetal oxygenation across the placenta and has clinical relevance in ventilation, anaesthesia, and acid-base disturbances, where acidosis and alkalosis shift the curve and alter how much oxygen the blood gives up to the tissues.

working.lead: Read acid as a release signal
working.text: expect rising carbon dioxide and falling pH to lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity and unload oxygen in the tissues.
expect low carbon dioxide and higher pH there to raise affinity and favour oxygen loading.

working.lead: Pair it with the Haldane effect
working.text: treat oxygen unloading in tissues and carbon dioxide pickup as linked, two sides of the same allosteric coupling.

limits: The Bohr effect is one of several modulators of the dissociation curve: 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate and temperature also shift it and are conceptually separate from the classic carbon-dioxide and pH effect, though often discussed together. It requires allosteric, multi-subunit hemoglobin, so monomeric myoglobin does not show it. It is a shift in affinity along a continuous sigmoidal curve, not an all-or-nothing switch. And extreme or pathological derangements of pH or carbon dioxide can compromise oxygen loading in the lungs, so the benefit is not unlimited.
misreadings: The effect is named for Christian Bohr, the physiologist, not his son Niels Bohr, the physicist. It should not be confused with the Haldane effect: the Bohr effect is the influence of carbon dioxide and acid on oxygen binding, while the Haldane effect is the influence of oxygen on carbon dioxide carriage. And it is not synonymous with the general shifts caused by 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate or temperature, which are separate modulators of the same curve.
origin: Described by the Danish physiologist Christian Bohr, working with Karl Hasselbalch and August Krogh, in 1904, from studies of how the carbon-dioxide tension of blood affects its oxygen binding.
